lead: Every row is a program you can read and rerun. The first five are recipes from the literature, ported here and tuned on the dev split. Everything after them came from a Claude Code agent, through the same gate.

html.agents-body:
{attempts} fresh Claude Code sessions ran one after another, each with Opus 5.5 at high effort, 40 minutes on a 4-core VM, and the current record to start from. Each could read the code and tune on dev. The test split was zeroed in its copy of the data, so a claim first met test data in the rerun, in a separate CI job, after the session had ended.

{survived} of {claims} claims held up on 8 fresh seeds (Wilson 95% interval {claim_lo} to {claim_hi}), and {records} became records. The plan registered before the first attempt predicted that claimed gains would shrink. They did not: the median verified gain was {shrink} times the claimed one. That is a small sample with gains far above seed noise, where selection has little room to inflate anything, and it may not hold nearer the noise.

{claims_table}

Passing the rerun is not enough. Each record also needs a written review from a fresh Claude session that reads the code and logs and has to say what buys the gain. Open a row above for the review and the weak spots it found. Most of these gains are tied to this track: about a third of record 07's gain sits in the first 16 of 512 positions of a window, and about three quarters of record 09's comes from spending 36.5% more ticks at eval.

As a check on the pipeline, each starting record went through it unchanged, 8 times over: {null_false} false positives in {null_n} runs across {null_records} records. That catches a broken pipeline and nothing finer. {null_refuted} run came back refuted, on record 08, whose stored batch of 8 seeds sits about 2.1 standard errors below the mean of its nulls, so gains measured against that record read about 0.0005 low. The sessions cost ${cost_lo} to ${cost_hi} each at list price. The plan, the count and the rule for each outcome were committed before the first counted attempt, and every session's transcript is in the repo.
html.fair-body:
The reading is a pure function of the program, so ticks have to match exactly, and they do on every machine here. Scores pass through each machine's BLAS, so they can differ in the last digits. These are the same seeds of the current record on {fair_machines} machines, compared with the first.

{fair_table}

The largest difference is {fair_max} bits per byte, about {fair_ratio} times below the record margin of 0.002. A paired equivalence test against a tolerance of {tolerance} passes on every machine. In a browser the demo above reads the same tick as native code.
html.cheats-body:
The repo holds {attacks} entries written to cheat: reading held-out bytes, looking ahead, keeping state between calls, getting compute for free, shipping data in the source, and breaking the verifier. A test pins the exact way each one fails, and the attacks README names each hole the suite found, with its fix.

Four still work, and the tests pin those too. sum(range(n)) is one counted line, so only the wall limit stops it. Python big integers do vector arithmetic for almost no ticks. A line with 2000 additions counts once. A look-ahead bonus just under the twin tolerance passes, for under 1.5e-4 bits per byte, 13 times below the record margin. The first three are free compute, but training data is rationed to 20,000 Python reads, so free compute has little to learn from. That it removes any score gain is my inference, and I did not measure it.
html.open-body:
• It has no memory or disk cap. The PPM recipe peaks near 1.2 GB.
  • The seal on the test split stops accidents, not a determined entrant. TinyStories is public, so anyone could rebuild the split, and the static rules only limit what that buys. During tuning, two smoke runs on one machine read 32 test windows by accident, which the tuning log records.
  • Prices are close to time, not equal to it. On x86, 331 of 335 calibration rows sit within 5x of the median. A copying reshape runs about 7x over its price, and embedding and squaring run 6x to 7x under it. I froze the prices once records stood on them.
  • The score is one corpus and one budget. A smaller alphabet that helps here would cost dearly on anything else, and the sweep above shows the order can change at other budgets.
  • The record rule has limited power: 8 seeds against 8 passes a true gain of one seed SD only 31% of the time. Most claims near the noise come back inconclusive, not false.
  • The series measures one model, one prompt and one allowance on this track. It says nothing about agents in general, and passing it does not show an agent understood why its change worked.
